desc:
You are given a text s and a dictionary. The dictionary is passed as one string words that lists distinct words separated by single commas.

Return true if s can be cut into one or more consecutive pieces so that every piece is a dictionary word. A word may be used any number of times (or not at all).

s = "applepenapple", words = "apple,pen"             -> true   (apple + pen + apple)
s = "catsandog",     words = "cats,dog,sand,and,cat" -> false
s = "aaaaaaa",       words = "aaaa,aaa"              -> true   (aaaa + aaa)
constraints: The whole words string has at most 5,000 characters
s and the words consist of lowercase English letters
hints: A greedy choice (always take the longest or shortest word) fails: with s = "aaaaaaa" and words aaaa, aaa you must plan ahead. Trying every cut recursively is correct but exponential.
Define ok[i] = 'the first i letters of s can be segmented'. The empty prefix is segmentable: ok[0] = true.
ok[i] is true if there is a cut j < i with ok[j] true and s[j:i] a dictionary word. Store the words in a set and only try piece lengths that occur in the dictionary.
editorial: This is a prefix DP. Let ok[i] be true when s[0:i] can be split into dictionary words, with ok[0] = true. For each end position i, look for a last piece s[j:i] that is a word such that ok[j] holds. The answer is ok[n].

Putting words in a hash set makes each membership test O(piece length). Only the distinct word lengths need to be tried as piece lengths, and there are at most 30 of them, so the running time is about O(n · (number of distinct lengths) · maxLen) instead of O(n²). Top-down recursion with memoisation on the start index is equivalent. A trie over the dictionary can replace the set and walks forward from each reachable position.
time: O(n * L * W) with L distinct word lengths, W max word length
